content: Healthcare services for cervical pre-cancer and cancer should be inclusive of transgender, intersex, and non-binary individuals. This inclusivity may necessitate additional training and sensitization of healthcare workers to address the unique needs of these populations. Public health authorities should prioritize these groups to improve awareness and access to cervical cancer screening and treatment. High-risk HPV DNA tests are used to identify carcinogenic HPV genotypes, typically including up to 14 types such as HPV 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, and 68. Among these, HPV 16 and 18 are the most carcinogenic and commonly associated with cervical cancers. Some tests provide specific information about HPV genotypes, such as HPV 16 and 18, while others offer partial genotyping, reporting HPV 16, 18, and sometimes HPV 45 separately from other carcinogenic types. Extended genotyping tests may include additional types like HPV 31, 33, 35, 45, 52, and 56. These tests help identify individuals at the highest risk of cervical cancer among those testing positive for HPV. HPV DNA testing can be performed using self-sampling or provider sampling methods. In this context, an HPV DNA test refers to a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for high-risk HPV. Cytology tests, including the Papanicolaou (Pap) smear and liquid-based cytology (LBC), detect atypical cervical cells through microscopic examination of prepared slides by trained experts. LBC requires advanced processing to create slides from liquid specimens. The threshold for further evaluation or treatment is a cytological result of atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASCUS) combined with the presence of high-risk HPV. Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) is not suitable for women where the transformation zone is no longer visible, such as postmenopausal women. Colposcopy, often used after a positive primary screening test, allows for detailed examination of the cervix to assess abnormalities and determine eligibility for ablative or excisional therapy. It may also facilitate biopsy or treatment when indicated. Colposcopy is not commonly used as a primary screening tool. Triage tests considered in these guidelines include high-risk HPV DNA partial genotyping, cytology, VIA, and colposcopy, with or without biopsy for histological diagnosis. Other triage tests are under clinical evaluation and may be added to future guidelines. Women who test HPV-negative are not treated or further evaluated, while those who test HPV-positive require assessment for eligibility for ablative treatment using acetic acid application and visual evaluation. Women ineligible for ablative treatment should be referred for excisional treatment or further evaluation. In a screen-and-treat approach, women who screen positive are treated without histological diagnosis. The goal of treatment is to destroy or remove the transformation zone of the cervix or areas identified as abnormal during screening. Ablative treatments do not provide tissue specimens for histological evaluation. Excisional treatments, such as large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ), are performed under local anesthesia in outpatient settings and yield tissue specimens for pathology. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued 23 recommendations and 7 good practice statements on cervical cancer screening and treatment. Among these, 6 recommendations are identical for the general population and women living with HIV, while 12 are specific to each group. WHO recommends starting regular cervical cancer screening at age 30 for the general population, with intervals of 5 to 10 years when using HPV DNA testing as the primary screening method. Priority should be given to women aged 30–49, and those aged 50–65 who have never been screened should also be prioritized when resources allow. HPV DNA testing is preferred over VIA or cytology as a primary screening test due to its higher sensitivity and greater reductions in cervical cancer incidence and mortality. Self-sampling for HPV DNA testing is considered comparable to provider-collected samples in detecting high-risk HPV. HPV DNA testing is also more cost-effective and acceptable to both women and providers, leading to more equitable access to screening. Conditional recommendations are made for using HPV DNA testing followed by treatment or triage testing, as the benefits and harms are similar for both approaches. The choice of triage method should depend on feasibility, training, program quality assurance, and available resources. Screening should continue until two consecutive negative results are obtained after age 50, with conditional recommendations for follow-up intervals based on modeling evidence. In summary, HPV DNA testing is the most effective and feasible method for cervical cancer prevention, offering significant benefits in reducing cancer incidence and mortality while being cost-effective and widely acceptable.
